solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plant bomb on dude

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece put on another follows it, so the fortune comes after the fellow

parts.note: a dude is a cool guy, which is jazz slang cat
a bomb is a fortune, which is also a mint

explanation.surface: A terrorist plants a bomb on some unsuspecting fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb about placing a bomb; it is the noun, the garden herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Catmint is a herbaceous garden perennial that cats love, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Gear — smack

explanation.surface: Drug slang: gear and smack are both street names for heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is British informal for one's clothes or kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber means kit or clothing in British slang, and to clobber someone is to wallop them.

clue.text: Legendary conflict's end in sight, first of twelve caught by arrow, unfortunately

indicators.note: the end in the word sight is its last letter
the month is caught, enclosed, by the jumbled weapon word
unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so the word arrow is jumbled

parts.note: January, Jan, is the first of the twelve months

explanation.surface: A legendary battle ends with the first of twelve soldiers shot by an arrow, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of twelve' is not a letter T but the first month of the year; 'end in sight' supplies the opening letter of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The war at Troy, told by Homer, is a conflict of myth and legend.

clue.text: Asian river is nearly dark, until show starts

indicators.note: the starts of the five words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A cinema-goer by an Asian river waits, as it is nearly dark, for the show to begin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus flows through Pakistan from Tibet, one of Asia's great rivers.

clue.text: Sign of Henry VIII barking out orders

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go mad into a new order

explanation.surface: King Henry VIII bellowing commands at his court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barking' (barking mad, British for crazy) is the anagram signal, not a description of shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-and-white rose was the heraldic emblem of Henry's royal house.

clue.text: Small bird shot with primitive weapon

parts.note: to have a shot at something is to have a go
a sling is an ancient weapon for hurling stones, as David used

explanation.surface: A little bird is brought down by somebody using a catapult.
explanation.definitionFit: A gosling is a young goose, a small bird not yet grown.

clue.text: Putting piece of cake into handbag, I'm meticulous!

indicators.note: the answer goes into, sits within, the run of letters of the following words

explanation.surface: Someone putting a piece of cake into a handbag claims to be meticulous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' is golf, not placing: a putt so short it is conceded.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a gimme is a short putt conceded as certain, an easy stroke.

clue.text: Thus, a time for contemporary music programme

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
pop is popular modern music
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: So, it is time for a modern-music programme on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' works like 'of': a time for pop is a pop era, which is why the music comes before the period.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera is a serial drama on television or radio, a type of broadcast show.

clue.text: Blooming thing hard, as are some setters?

parts.note: an iris is a flower, something that blooms
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A wry question whether some crossword setters are flowery and hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setters' are not puzzle-makers but the red dogs bred in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish setter is a breed of red gundog, so some setters come from Ireland.

clue.text: Fliers featuring no Italian

indicators.note: the birds feature, hold within them, the word no

parts.note: geese are birds, fliers

explanation.surface: A flight list with no Italian passengers.
explanation.definitionFit: A Genoese is a native of Genoa, a city in Italy, so is Italian.

clue.text: Ancient poet dressing old, curvy body

indicators.note: the poet's name dresses, or clothes, the letter for old by wrapping round it

parts.note: Ovid was a Roman poet of the Augustan age

explanation.surface: A Roman poet is putting clothes on an elderly, shapely figure.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovoid is an egg-shaped solid, a rounded three-dimensional body.

clue.text: Hell putting Mexico, perhaps, behind wall

indicators.note: the country piece goes behind, after, the barrier piece in the answer

parts.note: a dam is a wall holding back water
Mexico is an example of a nation, as 'perhaps' signals

explanation.surface: Building a wall on the Mexican border is pure hell, says the clue's political picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Damnation is eternal punishment, the condition of souls condemned to the underworld.

clue.text: French food about right, while service vacuous in restaurant

indicators.note: the cheese sits about, around, the other letters

parts.note: Brie is a French cheese
as can mean while, as in 'as he spoke'

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word service loses its insides and only its outer letters remain

explanation.surface: A diner complains that the French food was all right but the service was empty-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the cheese round the inner letters, which sit after its first letter; 'vacuous' keeps only the shell of service.
explanation.definitionFit: A brasserie is an informal French-style eating place serving simple meals.

clue.text: Brownish-yellow brooch, red clasps

indicators.note: the words brooch and red clasp, or hold, the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: A red brooch with clasps described in jewellery-catalogue language.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy pigment and the dull yellowish-brown colour named after it.

clue.text: Person in boat, one falling out with another?

definitions.meaning: a row is a quarrel, so one who rows argues; the rhyme with 'cower' is the second sense

explanation.surface: Two people in a boat, one tumbling overboard beside the other.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: one rhymes with 'mower', the other with 'power'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oarsman propels a boat; a quarreller is someone who has a row, a falling-out.

clue.text: Those second beans hard to reach?

definitions.meaning: people placed second in a contest
runner beans trained up tall canes, out of reach

explanation.surface: A gardener's second crop of beans is growing out of reach.
explanation.walkthrough: Runner beans are the British garden staple grown up canes, so runners up high are hard to reach.
explanation.definitionFit: The runners-up in a contest are those who finish second or behind the winner.

clue.text: A rave has gone out of control, typically

indicators.note: letters that are out of control run wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A wild party has spiralled out of control, as such parties usually do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link; the fodder is A RAVE plus GONE.
explanation.definitionFit: On average means usually or as a rule, which is what typically means.

clue.text: Unadulterated, funny show in the main sent up

indicators.note: the comedy show goes in the reversed water word
in a down clue sent up means written bottom to top, so read backwards

parts.note: the main is a poetic name for the sea
a sitcom is a situation comedy

explanation.surface: A comic programme mostly gets mocked, in its pure form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' pretends to mean mostly; here the main is the ocean, and 'sent up' turns it round before the comedy goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken as it comes means plain and undiluted, especially of a drink, so unadulterated.

clue.text: Alsatians mauled attacker

indicators.note: mauled letters are torn up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Guard dogs savaged someone who attacked.
explanation.definitionFit: An assailant is a person who assaults another, an aggressor.

clue.text: Fringes on eiderdown in worsted fabric, trim regularly plain

indicators.note: the edge letters go in the fabric word

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled worsted cloth

indicators.note: the fringes of a word are its edge letters, its first and last
taking letters regularly means every other one of the word trim

explanation.surface: A sewing instruction: put fringes on the eiderdown, in worsted fabric, and trim at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like needlework; only the last word is the definition, a noun for flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a vast grassland in Tanzania, a famous African plain.

clue.text: What to do with turkey? I give up!

definitions.meaning: a Christmas turkey is filled with stuffing
an exasperated cry of abandoning something

explanation.surface: A cook baffled by the Christmas bird throws in the towel.
explanation.definitionFit: Filling the bird with stuffing is what one does to it; 'stuff it' is also a cry of surrender.

clue.text: Tossing away odd bits of paper, sloppy old writer

indicators.note: throwing out the odd-numbered letters of the two words leaves the even ones

explanation.surface: A messy old author throws away scraps of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Across 'paper sloppy' the even letters are A, E, S, O, P.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek teller of fables, a writer of long ago.

clue.text: Smoker's articles confiscated by school

indicators.note: the articles are taken into the keeping of, enclosed by, the school word

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
the and a are the definite and indefinite articles

explanation.surface: A smoker's belongings are seized by the school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' is not a place of learning but a group of whales.
explanation.definitionFit: A pothead is slang for a habitual cannabis smoker.

clue.text: Free bet's non-starter, that is

indicators.note: a non-starter here is the wager word without its first letter

parts.note: a punt is a bet
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's free bet turns out to be a non-starter, that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like an adjective for the bet; it is the verb, release.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie something is to loosen its bonds and so set it free.

clue.text: Dry up above oxygen booster

indicators.note: in a down clue, above puts the first piece over the second
in a down clue up means written bottom to top, reversed

parts.note: brut describes very dry champagne
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A dried-up engine sits above an oxygen booster.
explanation.definitionFit: A turbo is a turbocharger, which boosts an engine's power.

clue.text: Rounding cape at sea, pale colour on one's cheeks etc

indicators.note: the word for pale goes round, encloses, the jumbled letters

parts.note: a faint colour is a pale one

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the word cape is jumbled

explanation.surface: A sailor rounding a cape at sea goes pale in the cheeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pale' looks like part of the seasick picture; it is the word that does the rounding, and 'at sea' is the jumble signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Face paint is make-up for decorating the face, colour applied to cheeks, forehead and so on.

clue.text: Defeat, as weakness picked up?

indicators.note: picked up means heard, as a signal is picked up

parts.note: a flaw is a weakness

explanation.surface: A defeat in which a weakness was spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to knock them down or beat them.

clue.text: Bows and ribbons perhaps finished with taffeta, finally

parts.note: past means over and done with

indicators.note: finally points to the final letter of taffeta

explanation.surface: Dressmaking: bows and ribbons are done, finished with taffeta.
explanation.walkthrough: Bows (farfalle) and ribbons (tagliatelle-like strips) are pasta shapes, not trimmings.
explanation.definitionFit: Bows and ribbons are shapes of Italian noodle dough, examples of the food.

clue.text: Devastating blow has one stop working in class

indicators.note: the pieces for one and resting go in the school-class word

parts.note: a form is a school class
I is the Roman numeral one
to rest is to stop working

explanation.surface: A schoolchild taking a break in class sounds like a devastating blow to learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A firestorm is an intense fire whipped up by its own winds, a destructive blast.

clue.text: Leg put on

definitions.meaning: a section of a journey or race
to present a play or event

explanation.surface: Someone has a leg put on, like a prosthetic fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg of a tour is one part of it; to put on a show is to mount it in a theatre.

clue.text: Case dispensed with, grog drunk by inebriate in private

indicators.note: the inner letters are swallowed, drunk, inside the drinker

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker

indicators.note: the outer letters of grog, its case, are dropped, leaving the middle

explanation.surface: A drunk privately downs grog after throwing away the crate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'private' looks like an adjective; it is the soldier of lowest rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier, especially in a cavalry or armoured regiment.

clue.text: With a long straight handle, screwed

definitions.meaning: having a shaft, as a tool or spear does
slang for cheated or badly let down

explanation.surface: A screwdriver with a long straight handle, screwed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool fitted with a shaft has a long handle; to be done over is to be ripped off.
